name: Beth Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on an underground crew for the big private utility in the city. Downtown, almost nothing is on poles, so we're in vaults under the pavement, pulling cable through ducts and splicing joints. A normal day is a traffic plan, a gas test on the vault, then hours in a hole about the size of a lift, with my journeyman checking every layer of my splice. It's fiddly, hot in summer and freezing in winter, and I'm still slow, but I like how exact it is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of it for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The splices. A medium-voltage joint has a dozen layers, and if one's wrong it fails in a year and someone's whole block goes dark. My journeyman, Kofi, makes me cut them open and start again, which I hate and also need. Owen, my partner, is an electrician on building sites, so we both come home filthy. We've got a small townhouse with a modest mortgage and about nine months of savings, which feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that, then. Back to work. I'd probably share some article about how the bubble burst, with a little eye-roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay sensible. The utility still needs cable splicers downtown, and there's a long list of old cable to replace. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the apprenticeship and focus on getting faster at splices. I'd keep using the AI chatbot now and then to check a spec or explain a theory question, because it's useful for that. And we'd keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries in this world at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company's private, and they're always talking about costs. Last year they froze apprentice hiring for six months. That's the kind of thing that could slow me down, but it wouldn't put me out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Owen do with the extra money in a calm year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the mortgage, take a proper holiday, maybe start thinking about kids in a couple of years. Nothing dramatic.

say: I'd shrug and say **back to work**.
I'd share an article about the **bubble bursting**, with an eye-roll.
think: Privately, the utility still needs **cable splicers** downtown for years.
There's a **long list** of old cable to replace.
do: Focus the apprenticeship on getting **faster at splices**.
Use the **AI chatbot** now and then to check specs.
feel: She feels **calm**, like it's a normal year.
S0.quote: The utility still needs cable splicers downtown, and there's a long list of old cable to replace.
fieldNote: Her pride is in **exact work**, and her worry is getting the splices right.
The real pressure is a **cost-cutting** private employer.
She and her partner have a **solid cushion** and modest mortgage.

steps.text: Practise medium-voltage splices until they pass first time
Use the AI chatbot to check cable specs now and then
Pay extra off the townhouse mortgage each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but it's manageable. People in the trades will be okay, and offices will need to adapt. I wouldn't post much, maybe something about helping people who lose jobs find new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my company would use it as an excuse. They'd put AI on the scheduling and the work orders, cut a few office jobs, and maybe slow down hiring apprentices again. I'm already in, so I'm safer than whoever comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new system they bring in, early-ish, once I see it works. I'd ask Kofi (my journeyman) to sign me off faster on the parts I'm good at, so I'm closer to a full ticket if they start cutting. And I'd keep the savings where they are, no big purchases this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, but the place would feel tighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does tighter look like, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer people in the office means more mistakes on our job sheets, which means crews sitting around waiting for a permit. And bosses who see a computer schedule and expect us to fit it, whatever's actually under the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners, mostly. There's a woman, Sunita, who knows where every old cable runs from memory. If the company replaces the planners with a system, the first time the map is wrong, it's my crew in the hole with a live cable.

say: I'd say it's **big but manageable**, and trades will be okay.
I'd maybe post about helping people **find new jobs**.
think: Privately, her company would use AI as an **excuse to cut** office jobs.
She's **already in**, so she's safer than future apprentices.
do: Learn the **new system** once she sees it works.
Ask her journeyman to **sign off faster** on parts she's mastered.
Hold off on any **big purchases** this year.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, because the workplace would feel tighter.
S1.quote: If the company replaces the planners with a system, the first time the map is wrong, it's my crew in the hole with a live cable.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **cost-cutting excuse** at a private utility.
She ties office cuts to **crew safety**, not just job loss.
Her plan is to **lock in her ticket** faster.

steps.text: Learn the new scheduling system once it proves itself
Ask her journeyman to sign off finished parts of the apprenticeship
Postpone big purchases and keep savings where they are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should slow it down, or at least make companies give notice. I'd say it online too, which I usually don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for both of us. The thinking stuff hits the office in 2028, but around 2031 robots come for hands-on work, and that's me in the vault and Owen on the building site. Two trades in one house, both on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and build cash instead, maybe to a year and a half. I'd look into cable testing and protection work, which is more about diagnosing faults, though AI might take that too. And Owen and I would put off kids for now, until we see what work looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We've got money, and I'm not falling apart, but two jobs at risk in one house is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, always. We'd cut holidays, eating out, Owen's new tools, everything else before we'd miss a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cable testing might go too. Why look at it, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the closest thing to my job that uses my head more than my hands. I honestly don't know if it's safer, but it's something to try. I'd rather do something than nothing.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should slow it down.
I'd push for companies to **give notice** before cuts.
think: Privately, **robots by 2031** hit both her and her partner's hands-on trades.
Two earners on the **same list** is the real fear.
do: Stop extra mortgage payments and build **cash to 18 months**.
Look into **cable testing** and protection work.
Put off **having kids** until work looks clearer.
feel: She feels **anxious** but not falling apart.
Having **two jobs at risk** in one house weighs on her.
S2.quote: Two trades in one house, both on that list.
fieldNote: Her mood is driven by the **household**, not only her own job.
She's honest that **cable testing** may not be safer.
Family plans are the first thing **put on hold**.

steps.text: Stop overpaying the mortgage and build cash to eighteen months
Ask about a move into cable testing and protection work
Put off having children with her partner for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan. Get unions and companies talking now about how robots come into the trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps me, I'd have my ticket and a few years in. But robots at 2034 still hit both of us, me and Owen, when we're in our mid-thirties and probably with a kid. That's the hard bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, keep saving, and take a cable testing course next year. I'd talk to Owen about one of us moving into something less hands-on by 2033. And I'd keep using AI tools for study, more than I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Less urgent, but the same worry underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would move, you or Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me, because I'm earlier in my trade. Owen's got eight years in, it's harder for him to start over. I'd tell him that over dinner and he'd argue, but he'd know I'm right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a kid change about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, honestly. I'd want one of us in something steady by then, even if it pays less.

I'd want **unions and companies** talking now.
think: She'd have her **ticket** by 2031, which helps.
Robots at **2034** still hit both earners in their mid-thirties.
do: Take a **cable testing course** next year.

feel: She's still **anxious**, with less urgency but the same worry.
S3.quote: I'd want one of us in something steady by then, even if it pays less.
fieldNote: She volunteers to be the one who **changes direction**.
A future **child** raises the stakes for her.
The worry is **structural**: two hands-on trades in one household.

steps.text: Take a cable testing course next year
Finish the apprenticeship and keep saving monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so it's on all of us to use it. Unions, companies, schools, everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes this feel normal. I'd be a journeyman for years, maybe a crew lead. Robots around 2039 are a long way off, and Owen and I would have time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, go back to paying extra on the mortgage, and maybe do the cable testing course in a few years. We'd go ahead with kids in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd feel we can handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it feel calm instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing what the robots can actually do. Ten years is long enough that I'd see the robots coming and know what's left for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you're learning now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools a bit more, the way the younger apprentices do. They're not afraid of it.

I'd call on **unions, companies and schools** to act.
think: Privately, ten years makes it **feel normal**, with years as a journeyman or crew lead.
Robots around **2039** give her and her partner plenty of time to plan.

Resume **extra mortgage payments** on the townhouse.
Plan to have **kids** in two or three years with her partner.
feel: She feels **slightly uneasy** but able to handle it.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd see the robots coming and know what's left for people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits both me and Owen within a few years. What would help is the company giving real notice, and some kind of funded course so one of us can move into testing or planning before the robots come.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about safety. If they cut planners and use maps from a computer, the people who pay for mistakes are the ones in the hole. That's us.

headlineQuote: If they cut planners and use maps from a computer, the people who pay for mistakes are the ones in the hole.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old apprentice** splicing underground cable for a private city utility.
She and her partner, an electrician, have a **townhouse** and about nine months saved.
She uses **AI now and then** to check specs and is open to proven tools.
She stays calm when nothing changes but grows **anxious** when robots threaten both trades.
Her plans for **children** move depending on how much warning there is.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it hits **both earners** in her household within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: Real **notice** from the company and a funded course to move into **testing or planning**.
